title: Douglas County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Douglas County wells run about 362 ft deep with a 12.5 gpm median yield. A typical new well here costs roughly $24,100-$37,300 finished.
h1: Understanding domestic wells in Douglas County, Colorado
intro_html:
In Douglas County you’re mostly dealing with Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and some fractured bedrock zones, so wells are real holes in the ground, not shallow sand points. Countywide, the median well depth is 362 feet, with the middle half between 234 and 550 feet and some going as deep as 3,220 feet.

There’s a big spread: about 13% of wells are under 100 feet, 44% run 300–600 feet, and 21% are over 600. That range is what drives the uncertainty in a driller’s bid if you’re buying land near Castle Rock, Parker, Franktown or the rural fringes.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Douglas County
sections.html:
Looking at the records, a “typical” Douglas County well is around 362 feet deep, but the depth band most buyers actually see is wider: the middle half fall between 234 and 550 feet. On the shallow end, 13% of wells are under 100 feet, often older or in favorable local geology. At the other extreme, 21% exceed 600 feet, and a few reach down as far as 3,220 feet.

The Denver Basin aquifers dominate here, with 92% of wells completed in Denver Basin units like the Upper Dawson and Denver aquifers, plus a lot of unnamed fractured-bedrock completions. That kind of bedrock means once the driller sets surface casing, they’re mostly hammering through rock, and small changes in location around places like The Pinery or Sterling Ranch can mean big depth differences.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water these wells make
sections.html:
Production in Douglas County is generally solid for domestic use. The median tested yield is 12.5 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. That’s more than enough for an exempt household well, which is limited by permit rules long before the pump runs out of capacity.

The distribution is encouraging: 65% of tested wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range, and 33% produce more than 15 gpm. Only 2% are down in the 1–5 gpm band, and none in the records show under 1 gpm. You still see variability in fractured bedrock, but countywide the risk of a truly marginal producer is relatively low compared with some mountain areas in nearby Elbert or Jefferson counties.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water level (the depth to water in the hole) has a median of 190 feet here, with the middle half between 101 and 364 feet. So in many Douglas County wells, you’re not pumping from the very bottom of a 500-foot hole; you’ve got a 100–300 foot water column above the pump when things are stable.

By decade, the trend has bounced around. Median water levels were about 140 feet in the 1950s, then 82 feet in the 1960s, dropping deeper to around 200 feet in the 1980s and about 305–300 feet in the 1990s–2000s. More recent records show shallower medians again, around 190 feet in the 2010s and 180 feet in the 2020s. That mix tells you localized drawdown and recovery patterns, not a simple straight-line decline, so it’s smart to compare your parcel with nearby wells in places like Grand View Estates or Highlands Ranch.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling and when
sections.html:
Douglas County has a long, steady drilling history. The Colorado Division of Water Resources shows 22,263 total well permits on record, with 12,631 recorded as constructed and 13,651 listing a total depth. Drilling picked up hard from the 1970s through the 2000s as Castle Rock, Parker, The Pinery and outlying areas grew.

By decade, permits climbed from 233 in the 1950s to 631 in the 1960s, then 3,312 in the 1970s and 3,464 in the 1980s. The 1990s saw 4,318 permits, tapering to 3,114 in the 2000s, 2,131 in the 2010s, and 1,252 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit dates into 2025, so drilling is ongoing. Hier Drilling Co Inc (Bruce Hier) and Hier Drilling Co. (Peter Hier) show up most often, along with “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” entries for licensed drillers working across the Denver Basin.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
On Douglas County’s Denver Basin bedrock, a realistic cost range is driven mainly by depth. Typical drilling rates run around $50–$70 per foot. At the county median depth of about 362 feet, that puts the bare hole in the ballpark of $18,100–$25,300.

Once you add pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical, a finished domestic well commonly lands around $24,100–$37,300 at that same depth. If you end up in one of the deeper zones, say in that 600+ foot group, you can scale those numbers up proportionally. When you’re budgeting a build in places like Franktown or rural Parker, assume at least the median case, and get a quote that spells out per-foot rates and materials so overruns are clear.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination and siting
sections.html:
The yield stats here are favorable, with no recorded wells under 1 gpm and only 2% between 1 and 5 gpm, but fractured bedrock is still unpredictable on a lot-by-lot basis. Always pull nearby well logs and look at both depth and yield before closing on land.

There are also mapped environmental concerns: roughly 127 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 31 historic mine features, and 18 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles in the county. That doesn’t mean your well is unsafe, but it does mean water testing is essential, especially near industrial or older developed areas around Castle Rock, Parker, or Highlands Ranch. For new builds, plan septic and well locations with enough separation and good slope so effluent can’t migrate toward your water source.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well in Douglas County
sections.html:
Permit records show 69% of wells here are domestic or household, 18% stock, 4% irrigation and 9% monitoring, so most rural homes are on standard exempt household permits. Those typically limit use to in-house plus some watered area if the parcel size and decree allow, not high-usage irrigation.

When you’re evaluating a lot near Stonegate, Meridian Village, Sierra Ridge or out toward the county lines with Arapahoe or Elbert, focus on three things: depth and yield of adjacent wells, water level trend over time, and any nearby contamination or historic mining. Confirm the existing permit type and actual constructed depth against state records, and budget realistically using the county’s 234–550 foot “middle half” depth band, not just an optimistic shallow neighbor.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Douglas County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across Douglas County, the median well depth is about 362 feet. The middle half of wells fall between 234 and 550 feet, with 44% in the 300–600 foot band. About 13% of wells are under 100 feet, while 21% are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well goes down to about 3,220 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Douglas County wells typically produce?
faq.a: Tested pump yields in Douglas County are generally strong. The median yield is 12.5 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. Around 65% of wells produce 5–15 gpm, and 33% exceed 15 gpm. Only about 2% of wells are in the 1–5 gpm range, and none in the records show under 1 gpm.

faq.q: Is the groundwater level dropping in Douglas County?
faq.a: The long-term picture is mixed. Median static water levels were about 140 feet in the 1950s, shallowed to 82 feet in the 1960s, then deepened to around 200 feet in the 1980s and roughly 305–300 feet in the 1990s–2000s. More recent medians improved to about 190 feet in the 2010s and 180 feet in the 2020s, so it’s not a simple steady decline.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Douglas County, CO?
faq.a: On Denver Basin bedrock, typical drilling runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 362 feet, the drilled hole comes out roughly $18,100–$25,300. A complete domestic well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical commonly totals around $24,100–$37,300 at that depth, with deeper sites costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Douglas County?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location. Records show about 127 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 31 historic mine features and 18 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Many private wells are fine, but you should always test for common contaminants and any site-specific concerns before relying on a Douglas County well for drinking water.
